subject: Respiratory failure
object: when the respiratory system fails to carry out its gas exchange functions, which include oxygenation and removing carbon dioxide.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Respiratory failure is defined as the failure of the respiratory system to perform its gas exchange functions, including oxygenation and carbon dioxide elimination.

subject: Acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, also called type 1,
object: oxygenation failure and refers to de novo respiratory failure, that is, excluding hypoxaemia caused by cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and exacerbations of chronic lung disease; the main cause of such de novo respiratory failure is pneumonia.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, also referred to as type 1, specifically denotes oxygenation failure and refers to de novo respiratory failure, i.e. excluding hypoxemia caused by cardiogenic pulmonary edema and exacerbation of chronic lung diseases. The main etiology of such de novo respiratory failure is pneumonia .

subject: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, also called type 2,
object: a ventilation failure defined by an arterial carbon dioxide pressure (PaCO2) above 45 mm Hg and a pH below 7.35, indicating respiratory acidosis, and is not included in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Thus, acute hypoxemic respiratory failure does not encompass acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, also referred to as type 2, characterized by a ventilation failure defined by arterial carbon dioxide pressure (PaCO 2) exceeding 45 mm Hg and pH below 7.35, indicative of respiratory acidosis.

subject: According to the expert panel for these oxygen therapy guidelines, acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure
object: a PaO2 below 60 mm Hg or an SpO2 below 90% on room air, or a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 300 mm Hg or less in patients receiving oxygen therapy.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: According to the panel of experts participating in these guidelines on oxygen therapy , acute hypoxemic respiratory failure can be defined as partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO 2) less than 60 mm Hg or peripheral oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry (SpO 2) less than 90% on room air, or a ratio of the partial pressure of arterial oxygen to the fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO 2 /FiO 2) of 300 mm Hg or less ratio less in patients receiving oxygen therapy.

subject: When FiO2 is not measured under conventional oxygen therapy through nasal cannula or face mask, it
object: with the formula FiO2 (%) = oxygen flow (L/min) × 3 + 21%.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Whereas FiO 2 is not measured under conventional oxygen therapy (COT) delivered through nasal cannula or facemask, it can be best estimated using the following formula: FiO 2 in % = Flow of oxygen (L/min) x 3 + 21% .

subject: Whatever the oxygenation strategy, hypoxaemia
object: severe at a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 100 mm Hg or below, moderate at 101 to 200 mm Hg and mild at 201 to 300 mm Hg, as in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Regardless of the oxygenation strategy, hypoxemia can be considered as severe in patients with PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio equal to or below 100 mm Hg, moderate in patients with PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio between 101 and 200 mm Hg, and mild in patients with PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio between 201 and 300 mm Hg, as in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) .

subject: Clinical signs of acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure
object: a respiratory rate above 25 breaths per minute, use of the accessory respiratory muscles, paradoxical abdominal breathing, cyanosis, dyspnoea and breathlessness.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Clinical signs of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure include increased respiratory rate above 25 breaths per minute, activation of accessory respiratory muscles, paradoxical abdominal respiration, cyanosis, dyspnea, and breathlessness.

source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Among patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, a vast majority have pulmonary bilateral infiltrates on chest radiograph and could be considered as having ARDS criteria . However, as the Berlin definition of ARDS stated that PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio had to be measured with positive airway pressure of at least 5 cmH 2 O , patients treated with COT or HFNC still cannot be considered as ARDS .

source_quote: In a large retrospective cohort study including 152,680 patients admitted to 150 ICUs, hypoxemia occurring within the first 24 h following admission was associated with an increased risk of death .

source_quote: Animal studies have consistently shown that exposure to high FiO 2 can cause respiratory failure and early death . Whereas ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) is well- established , the specific pulmonary lesions attributable to oxygen toxicity remain hypothetical.

source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Additionally, in a large retrospective cohort study including 19,593 patients admitted to five ICUs in the United Kingdom, exposure to hyperoxia (defined as PaO 2 ≥ 100 mm Hg), no matter its duration, increased risk of death when compared to patients non-exposed to hyperoxia .

subject: Oxygen
object: a treatment for hypoxaemia, not breathlessness, and supplemental oxygen does not improve dyspnoea and breathlessness in patients who are not hypoxaemic.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Oxygen is a treatment for hypoxemia, not breathlessness, and supplemental oxygen does not improve dyspnea and breathlessness in non-hypoxemic patients .

subject: The accuracy of SpO2 measurement
object: technical problems and measurement biases such as low peripheral blood flow, anaemia and skin pigmentation, and SpO2 can differ considerably between monitoring devices, with errors from −3% to +1% compared with arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2).
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: However, technical problems and measurement biases, such as low peripheral blood flow, anemia, and skin pigmentation can significantly compromise the accuracy of SpO 2 measurements . Moreover, there may be considerable discrepancies in SpO 2 measurements between different monitoring devices, with errors ranging from − 3% to + 1% relative to arterial oxygen saturation (SaO 2) as the reference .

subject: In patient self-inflicted lung injury with non-invasive respiratory support, patients producing strong inspiratory efforts
object: large tidal volumes under non-invasive ventilation, which may worsen lung injury by increasing transpulmonary pressures, in the same way that large tidal volumes are harmful in patients with ARDS on invasive mechanical ventilation.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Patient self-inflicted lung injury associated with noninvasive respiratory supports Patients producing strong inspiratory efforts generate large tidal volumes under NIV, and that may lead to worsening of lung injury by increasing transpulmonary pressures, in the same way that large tidal volumes are harmful in patients with ARDS under invasive mechanical ventilation .

subject: Although tidal volumes do not increase when switching from conventional oxygen to high-flow nasal oxygen, patients with strong inspiratory efforts
object: lung injury, whatever the type of non-invasive respiratory support.
source: Article: Thille AW, Balen F, Carteaux G et al. Oxygen therapy and noninvasive respiratory supports in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: a narrative review. Annals of Intensive Care 2024
source_quote: Although tidal volumes do not increase when switching form COT to HFNC , patients with strong inspiratory efforts could still develop lung injury, regardless of the type of noninvasive respiratory support .

subject: Patients with acute respiratory failure
object: gas exchange derangements that may result in hypercapnia.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: Patients with acute respiratory failure almost always develop gas exchange derangements that may result in hypercapnia .

subject: Both hypercapnia and hypercapnic acidosis
object: the haemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve to the right and may increase haematocrit, increasing oxygen release to the tissues in a canine model; hypercapnia also increases cardiac output through sympathoadrenal mechanisms, with increased preload, afterload, contractility and heart rate, and the overall effect is better oxygenation and improved global oxygen supply.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: Both hypercapnia and hypercapnic acidosis shift the hemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve to the right and may increase hematocrit, augmenting the release of oxygen to the tissues in a canine model . It also increases cardiac output through sympathoadrenal mechanisms . The secondary rise in cardiac output is associated with increased preload, afterload, contractility, and elevated heart rate . The overall effect is better oxygenation and improved global oxygen supply.

subject: Hypercapnia
object: alveolar oxygen tension, by the formula PAO2 = FiO2 (PB − 47) − (PaCO2/R), where PAO2 is the alveolar oxygen tension, PB the barometric pressure and R the respiratory quotient; however, compared with changes in FiO2, the effect of changes in alveolar ventilation on alveolar oxygenation is small.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: On the other hand, hypercapnia lowers alveolar oxygen tension by the following formula P A O 2 = FiO 2 (P B -47)—(PaCO 2 / R), where P A O 2 is the alveolar oxygen tension, P B is the barometric pressure, and R is the respiratory quotient. However, compared to alterations in FiO 2 , the effect on alveolar oxygenation by alterations in alveolar ventilation is small.

subject: Hypercapnia
object: airway resistance: alveolar hypercapnia decreases it by relaxing the smooth muscle of small bronchi (a direct effect) in healthy subjects, while systemic hypercapnia causes vagally mediated constriction of the larger airways (an indirect effect) in animal models, and these opposing but balanced effects may produce little net change in airway resistance.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: Hypercapnia may either decrease or increase airway resistance. Alveolar hypercapnia decreases airway resistance by relaxing smooth muscle small bronchi (a direct effect) in healthy subjects , while systemic hypercapnia causes vagal nerve-mediated constriction of the larger airway (an indirect effect) in animal models . These opposing but balanced effects may produce a little net alteration in airway resistance .

subject: Hypercapnia
object: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, reducing intrapulmonary shunt and improving gas exchange in normal and diseased lungs.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: Hypercapnia potentiates hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with a reduction in intrapulmonary shunt, improving gas exchange in normal and diseased lungs .

subject: Hypercapnic acidosis
object: diaphragmatic function in spontaneously breathing patients, through effects on afferent transmission by the vagal nerve.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: However, hypercapnic acidosis impairs diaphragmatic function in spontaneously breathing patients, through effects on afferent transmission by the vagal nerve .

subject: In a post hoc analysis of three prospective non-interventional international studies in ARDS patients, severe hypercapnia (PaCO2 above 50 mm Hg)
object: higher mortality and more organ failures than normocapnia, and acidosis, or hypercapnia combined with acidosis, independently increased the risk of death in the intensive care unit.
source: Article: Morales-Quinteros L, Camprubí-Rimblas M, Bringué J et al. The role of hypercapnia in acute respiratory failure. Intensive Care Medicine Experimental 2019
source_quote: Recently, a post hoc analysis of three prospective non-interventional international studies in ARDS patients was published . In this analysis, severe hypercapnia (PaCO 2 > 50 mmHg) was associated with higher mortality and more organ failures compared to patients with normocapnia. Acidosis or the combination of hypercapnia and acidosis independently increased the risk of mortality in the intensive care unit.
